title: Regional accents and dialects

blocks.x: This was before we exploded into the world scene, before computers and before jet airplanes. They had everything else, I guess but it was still regional because in those days people from Chicago had a definite dialect, people from Boston did, people from Kansas City did and this was reflected in the music they did.
I think that's still true to an extent.
Not so much. I remember Chicago had an accent that was very thick, and Kansas City was another one. Bobby Brookmayer's got a touch of it.
When I moved to New York from Ohio, I really got a lot of

ribbing for the longest time because of my "accent", and believe me, if any of my New York friends, people who were born and raised in the New York area, went out to the midwest, they'd probably go through the same thing.
You still get the Brooklynese here, but it's not like it used to be. I would say that yours is a general accent. How long have you been here?
I have lived in New York in the early seventies and I was in Washington five years.
You have a middle western aura still, but it's not that noticeable.
I don't hear that much of it anymore as I go around the country. It seems to have leveled off.
I'm told that apparently that an anchorman, a TV newsman, for TV networks, the ideal people to get are

people from the midwest, because the mid-western dialect or whatever--this is all getting approval from Eddie's wife--apparently the midwestern dialect is the most general and the most generally pleasing to a nation-wide audience, or whatever.
I was told many times when I moved to New York that I talk weird.
It's not so bad as it used to be. I often wondered about that.

When we went to Europe in '57, we went on a Dutch boat, there were bilingual announcements and it suddenly occurred to me that the Brooklyn accent is a Dutch accent, that the whole area has this and this was originally colonized by the Dutch.
That's true.
It's weird how long ago that was and how it sticks. Boston is Old English--

--Boston is Old English and it's very close, in a certain way--
Oh, yeah, Boston people you can really tell.
Not so much anymore. I think the colleges may have done that. They're not as regional as they used to be. North Carolina, wow, the backwoods down there, which is again British, but of another period.
